documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.statement:
The following eight steps describe the procedure for analysing an alloy containing tin and lead.

1. Dissolve a 0.4062 g sample by heating in a small beaker with a mixture of 11 M hydrochloric and 16 M nitric acid until the entire alloy dissolves. Lead is oxidised to Pb(II) and tin becomes Sn(IV).
2. Heat for five minutes to expel oxides of nitrogen and chlorine. Some acid remains. On cooling, a precipitate of some tin compounds and a lead compound appears.
3. Add a 25.00 cm³ aliquot of 0.2000 M Na₂H₂EDTA. The precipitate dissolves and a clear, colourless solution is obtained.
4. Transfer quantitatively to a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask and make up to the mark with distilled water.
5. Treat a 25.00 cm³ aliquot with 15 cm³ of 30% w/v hexamine (hexamethylenetetramine), some water and two drops of Xylenol Orange solution. The pH of each aliquot is 6.
6. Titrate this clear yellow solution with standard 0.009970 M lead nitrate until the colour just changes from yellow to red. The titre is 24.05 cm³.
7. Add 2.0 g of solid NaF to the titration flask. The solution turns back to yellow.
8. Titrate with more standard 0.009970 M lead nitrate until the colour changes to red again. This titre is 15.00 cm³.

Hexamine and Xylenol Orange have the structures below. Hexamine has $\mathrm{p}K_b=9.5$. Xylenol Orange is red below pH 4 and yellow above pH 5.

![](p1-fig1)

$K'_{\mathrm{MY}}=\alpha K_{\mathrm{MY}}$ is the conditional formation constant. The figure shows $K'_{\mathrm{MY}}$ for EDTA complexes of Pb(II) and Sn(IV), with and without fluoride.

![](p1-fig2)

parts.statement: What is the lead compound that precipitates in step 2?
Write a balanced ionic equation explaining the disappearance of the precipitate in step 3, at pH 6.
What is the purpose of hexamine in step 5?
What is the purpose of Xylenol Orange?
Write balanced ionic equations for the reactions during the titration and responsible for the colour change at the endpoint in step 6.
What is the purpose of NaF in step 7?
Write a balanced ionic equation for the reaction in step 7.
Write a balanced ionic equation explaining why the colour changes from red to yellow in step 7.
Write a balanced ionic equation explaining why the Pb + EDTA and Pb + EDTA + F⁻ lines on the $\log K_{\mathrm{MY}}$ versus pH graph coincide below pH 2.
Calculate the percentages by weight of Sn and Pb in the alloy.

sections.statement: PbCl₂, or any hydroxo species, etc.

$$
\mathrm{PbCl_2(s)+H_2Y^{2-}\longrightarrow PbY^{2-}+2H^++2Cl^-},
$$

or similar.
It forms a pH buffer.
It is a metallochromic indicator.

(i) During titration:

$$
\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+H_2Y^{2-}\longrightarrow PbY^{2-}+2H^+}.
$$

(ii) At the endpoint, a slight excess of Pb²⁺ forms a red complex with Xylenol Orange:

$$
\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+XO\ (yellow)\longrightarrow PbXO^{2+}\ (red)}.
$$
NaF forms a complex with tin.

The graph shows that fluoride forms a stable complex with Sn⁴⁺ but not Pb²⁺ at pH 6, displacing EDTA:

$$
\mathrm{SnY+nF^-+2H^+\longrightarrow SnF_n^{(n-4)-}+H_2Y^{2-}},
\qquad n\text{ typically }4\text{–}6.
$$

Released EDTA destroys the small amount of red PbXO complex, producing free yellow XO. The charge on XO is ignored.

$$
\mathrm{H_2Y^{2-}+PbXO^{2+}\longrightarrow PbY^{2-}+XO\ (yellow)+2H^+}.
$$

Below pH 2, F⁻ is protonated and does not compete effectively with Y for Pb²⁺:

$$
\mathrm{H^++F^-\longrightarrow HF}.
$$

EDTA in excess, determined from the standard Pb²⁺ titrant:

$$
n(\mathrm{EDTA})=n(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}})
=0.02405\ \mathrm{dm^3}\times0.009970\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}
=2.398\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

The original EDTA amount is printed as

$$
n(\mathrm{EDTA})_{\mathrm{init}}
=0.1\times25.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\times0.2000\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}
=5.000\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

EDTA consumed by Pb²⁺ and Sn⁴⁺ in a 25 cm³ aliquot:

$$
n(\mathrm{EDTA})_{\mathrm{consumed}}
=(5.000-2.398)\times10^{-4}
=2.602\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}
=n(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}+Sn^{4+}}).
$$

EDTA released from SnY by fluoride is printed as

$$
n(\mathrm{EDTA})_{\mathrm{released}}
=n(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}})_{\mathrm{stand}}
=15.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}\times0.009970\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}
=1.496\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}
=n(\mathrm{Sn^{4+}}).
$$

Therefore, in the 25 cm³ aliquot,

$$
n(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}})=(2.602-1.496)\times10^{-4}
=1.106\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

In the original 0.4062 g alloy sample:

$$
m(\mathrm{Sn})=10(1.496\times10^{-4})(118.69)=0.1776\ \mathrm{g},
$$

$$
m(\mathrm{Pb})=10(1.106\times10^{-4})(207.19)=0.2292\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

$$
\mathrm{Sn}:\ 100\frac{0.1776}{0.4062}=43.7\%,\qquad
\mathrm{Pb}:\ 100\frac{0.2292}{0.4062}=56.4\%.
$$

problems.title: Problem 2

sections.title: Part A: Dating Historical Events Using Pb-210
sections.statement:
Nathan Thompson, one of the first inhabitants of Lord Howe Island, planted some European deciduous trees in his garden. The exact time of planting is unknown. Over the years, pollen from the European oak and elm accumulated at the bottom of the lake near his house. Very small quantities of radioactive Pb-210, with half-life 22.0 years, were deposited at the same time. European oak and elm pollinate in their first year of growth.

In 1995, researchers sampled a sediment core from the lake bottom, cut it into 1 cm slices and examined the slices for pollen and radioactive Pb-210. They found:

- European oak and elm pollen first occurs at a depth of 50 cm.
- Pb-210 activity is 356 Bq/kg at the top and 1.40 Bq/kg at 50 cm.

parts.statement:
In what year did Nathan Thompson plant the seeds?

Pb-210 is a daughter of U-238. U-238 occurs in the earth's crust; some Pb-210 rains out of the atmosphere and attaches to sediment particles accumulating at lake bottoms. The printed abbreviated decay chain is

$$
\mathrm{U\!-\!238\longrightarrow U\!-\!234\longrightarrow Th\!-\!230
\longrightarrow Ra\!-\!226\longrightarrow Rn\!-\!222
\longrightarrow(Po\!-\!218\longrightarrow Bi\!-\!214)^*
\longrightarrow Pb\!-\!210\longrightarrow Pb\!-\!206\ (stable)}.
$$

The starred nuclides have very short half-lives: minutes and days.
Which step explains how Pb-210 reaches rainwater while its parent U-238 occurs only in the earth's crust?

sections.title: Part B: Separation of Radionuclides for Nuclear Medicine Applications
sections.statement:
Ga-67 is used to image lymphoma. It is preferentially produced by bombarding a Zn-68-enriched target, greater than 98%, with high-energy protons for 11 hours. Natural Zn-68 abundance is 18.8%. Target design allows production of other radionuclides. Twelve hours after bombardment, Ga-67 is bound on a cation exchange. Other radionuclides and Zn-68 are eluted in the wash solution, leaving Ga-67 on the column.

**Table 1**

| Radionuclide | Half-life |
| --- | --- |
| Co-55 | 18.2 hr |
| Ni-57 | 36.0 hr |
| Co-57 (daughter of Ni-57) | 270 days |
| Cu-64 | 12.7 hr |
| Cu-67 | 61.7 hr |
| Zn-65 | 244 days |
| Ga-67 | 78.35 hr |
| Ga-66 | 9.4 hr |

Cu-64 and Co-55 have ideal half-lives for nuclear medicine, so isolating them from the wash solution would be useful.

The distribution coefficient $D$ measures partition of a metal ion between ion-exchange resin and eluant:

$$
D=\frac{\text{radioactivity per mg of resin}}
{\text{radioactivity per cm}^3\text{ of eluant}}.
$$

Reasonable separation requires the two ions' $D$ values to differ by at least 10 units.

![](p2-fig1)

![](p2-fig2)

parts.statement: Evaporate the wash solution to dryness, resuspend in a small amount of 0.2 M HCl in 96% methanol, and load onto an anion-exchange column. Use figures 1 and 2 to rank the best solvent systems, from the given alternatives, for eluting Cu-64 and Co-55.

Long-lived radionuclides may interfere with medical use of Cu-64, Co-55 or Ga-67. Mark each statement true or false; one or more may be true.

a) Ni-57 may be present as a contaminant of Co-55.

b) Co-57 will interfere with medical use of Co-55.

c) Cu-67 will interfere with medical use of Cu-64.

d) Ga-66 will interfere with use of Ga-67.

e) Ga-67 will interfere with medical use of Cu-64.

Which methods reduce radionuclide contaminants of Cu-64, Co-55 or Ga-67? Mark each statement true or false; one or more may be true.

a) Remove Ni-57 before isolating Co-55.

b) Separate Ni-57 from the bombarded target material before isolating Ga-67.

c) Separate radionuclides closer to the end of bombardment.

d) Allow Ni-57 to decay before isolating Co-55.

If naturally abundant zinc replaces enriched Zn-68 during proton bombardment, mark each statement true or false; one or more may be true.

a) Ga-67 would be produced at fivefold higher yields.

b) Ga-67 would be produced at fivefold lower yields.

c) Ga-67 would have lower yields and contamination by Cu-64, Co-55, Co-57 and Ni-57 would increase.

d) Ga-67 would have lower yields and contamination by Cu-64, Co-55, Co-57 and Ni-57 would remain the same.

sections.statement:
The printed apparent-decay sequence over 50 cm is

$$
356-178-89-44.5-22.5-11.25-5.63-2.81-1.39.
$$

This represents eight half-lives, or $8\times22=176$ years. The planting year is $1995-176=1819\ (\pm2)$.

The four alternatives are printed in the solution, with boxes for ranks 1–4 (1 best):

| Alternative | Elution sequence |
| --- | --- |
| A | 0.2 M HCl / 96% methanol to remove Ni-57; then 2.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Cu-64; then 1.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Co-55 |
| B | 0.2 M HCl / 96% methanol to remove Ni-57; then 2.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Co-55; then 1.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Cu-64 |
| C | 2.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Co-55; then 1.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Cu-64 |
| D | 0.2 M HCl / 96% methanol to remove Ni-57; then 3.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Co-55; then 4.0 M HCl / 55% isopropyl alcohol to remove Cu-64 |

Best sequence: **B, C, D, A**.

The sequences **B, C, A, D**, **C, B, D, A** and **C, B, A, D** were also accepted, with fewer points.
a) False; b) True; c) True; d) False; e) False.
a) True; b) True; c) True; d) False.
a) False; b) True; c) False; d) True.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.statement:
Three-dimensional polycyclic molecular structures can often be explained by minimising angle strain. Consider dodecahedrane, C₂₀H₂₀, and ovalene, C₃₂H₁₄:

![](p3-fig1)

![](p3-fig2)

Each C₅ ring of dodecahedrane is a regular pentagon; each C₆ ring of ovalene can be regarded as a regular hexagon.

parts.statement: What are the $\angle(\mathrm{CCC})$ angles for each ring?
Which configuration most closely matches these angles: trigonal planar, 120°; tetrahedral, 109.5°; or octahedral, 90°?

Which hybridization, sp, sp² or sp³, most closely conforms to dodecahedrane and ovalene?

A **juncture** means any three-ring system sharing a common central carbon atom within a molecule. Compare the bold junctures of three pentagons in dodecahedrane and three hexagons in ovalene.

![](p3-fig3)

![](p3-fig4)

Consider an axis through the central carbon of each juncture making an identical angle with all three radiating C–C bonds.

![](p3-fig5)
What is this angle for dodecahedrane, making an educated guess to the nearest three degrees, and for ovalene?

Subtracting 90° describes each juncture's deviation from planarity. Which juncture is planar?

Now consider the polycyclic alkenes dodecahedrene, C₂₀H₁₈, and ovalene:

![](p3-fig6)

![](p3-fig7)

Assume a rigid molecular framework, not significantly distorted by H₂ addition at the indicated double bond. Assume all double bonds are localized in assessing these systems.

Compare the encircled carbon pairs. For which C=C pair is H₂ addition expected to be more exothermic?

For all known fullerenes, deviation from planarity at any juncture is less than for dodecahedrane.

![](p3-fig8)

All C₆₀ junctures are equivalent. Consider H₂ addition at a C=C bond:

![](p3-fig9)
For which of C₆₀, dodecahedrene or ovalene is H₂ addition most exothermic? Again assume localized double bonds.

For which is H₂ addition least exothermic?

There is evidence for fullerenes smaller than C₆₀, such as C₅₈. Ignoring distinctions between single and double bonds:

![](p3-fig10)

The junctures around A, B and C are redrawn for clarity:

![](p3-fig11)
Which juncture has the least deviation from planarity?
Which has the greatest deviation from planarity?

Which of bonds 1–9 is the most favourable site for H₂ addition?

Finally, consider the larger fullerene C₁₈₀:

![](p3-fig12)

To a first approximation, C₆₀ and C₁₈₀ are perfect spheres.
Which has the larger average deviation from planarity at each juncture?

Compare C₆₀, C₁₈₀ and graphite geometries. Which statement on the answer sheet about enthalpies of formation, in $\mathrm{kJ\,g^{-1}}$, is correct?

Fullerenes form on a very rapid timescale, typically milliseconds. All techniques produce much more C₆₀ than C₁₈₀.

Which graph on the answer template best represents potential energy versus reaction progress for

$$
\mathrm{reactants\rightleftharpoons3C_{60}},\qquad
\mathrm{reactants\rightleftharpoons C_{180}}?
$$

sections.statement: Dodecahedrane: 108°. Ovalene: 120°.

Dodecahedrane: tetrahedral. Ovalene: trigonal planar.

The dodecahedrane CCC angle is only slightly below the tetrahedral angle, well above octahedral 90°, and too low for trigonal planar geometry. Ovalene's angle equals the trigonal planar angle.

Dodecahedrane: sp³. Ovalene: sp².

Dodecahedrane closely conforms to a tetrahedral arrangement at each carbon; ovalene corresponds exactly to a trigonal planar arrangement.

Dodecahedrane, C₂₀H₂₀: 109–115 degrees. Ovalene, C₃₂H₁₄: 90 degrees.

The three dodecahedrane rings are not coplanar. Determining the exact axis angle is complicated, but the C₅ ring CCC angle is very close to tetrahedral. Distortion at each carbon is slight, so the axis angle is about 109.5°; the source prints **“more probably –112°”**. Ovalene's rings are coplanar, making the axis angle 90°.
Ovalene, C₃₂H₁₄.

H₂ addition is more exothermic for dodecahedrene.

Its C=C pair is more suited to sp³ than sp², favouring dihydrogenation to dodecahedrane. Ovalene favours sp² over sp³, so angle strain disfavors addition at the indicated site. Reduction of aromaticity also likely disfavors hydrogenation, independently of this angle-strain argument.

Dodecahedrene gives the most exothermic H₂ addition.

A C₆₀ juncture deviates less from planarity than dodecahedrene, whose carbons are close to tetrahedral sp³, but more than flat sp² ovalene. C₆₀ is intermediate in its preference for hydrogenated versus dehydrogenated structures.

Dodecahedrene junctures are $[\mathrm{C_5,C_5,C_5}]$; ovalene junctures are $[\mathrm{C_6,C_6,C_6}]$; C₆₀ junctures are $[\mathrm{C_5,C_6,C_6}]$. More pentagons imply greater deviation from planarity and greater relative stability of sp³ rather than sp² at the central carbon.
Ovalene gives the least exothermic H₂ addition.
B has the least deviation from planarity.

C has the greatest deviation.

A has two hexagons and a pentagon, the pattern of the fullerene junctures called **“Ceo”** in this printed line. B has three hexagons; C has two pentagons and a hexagon. Increasing pentagon count gives increasing deviation, greatest at C and least at B.

Bond 9 is the most favourable H₂-addition site.

Bonds 1, 2, 7 and 8 lie between a pentagon and a hexagon; bonds 3–6 lie between two hexagons. Bond 9 lies between adjacent pentagons. It is most distorted from the planarity favoured by sp² and closest to the dodecahedrane skeleton, nearly ideal for sp³, favouring dihydrogenation.

C₆₀ has the larger average deviation.

C₁₈₀ has a larger diameter and smaller average deviation at each juncture. Its equator contains more atoms than the C₆₀ equator.

$$
\Delta_fH^0(\mathrm{C_{60}})
>\Delta_fH^0(\mathrm{C_{180}})
>\Delta_fH^0(\text{graphite}).
$$

C₆₀ has greater average deviation than C₁₈₀, making sp² less favourable in the smaller fullerene. Both are nonplanar and less amenable to sp² than graphite. Graphite also receives stabilization from interlayer electronic effects; that last point is not required for the answer.

All five alternative graphs are printed in the key:

![](p3-sol-fig1)

![](p3-sol-fig2)

The best graph is **a**.

The equilibrium line is printed as

$$
\mathrm{C_{60}\rightleftharpoons reactants\rightleftharpoons3C_{60}}.
$$

The key describes a large positive energy change from left to middle and a smaller negative change from middle to right. Formation of C₁₈₀ is thermodynamically favoured over three C₆₀ molecules. Predominant C₆₀ indicates kinetic control and insufficient time to reach equilibrium.
